prompt: With `Channel` in Rows and `Revenue` in Values, what does the pivot show as the Sum of Revenue for `Online`?
hint: Check it with a SUMIFS on the Channel column.

prompt: Why can a pivot table not forget a channel, the way a grid of hand-typed `SUMIFS` can?
hint: Where does the list of channels in the pivot come from?

choices.text: It lists the values it finds
choices.why: Right. A SUMIFS grid has a row only for each channel somebody remembered to write.

choices.text: It checks the channels against a list kept in Excel's options
choices.why: There is no such list; the pivot reads the data.

choices.text: It refuses to build if a channel is missing
choices.why: Nothing is missing from a pivot's point of view; it shows what is there.

choices.text: It always shows exactly three channels
choices.why: It shows as many as the column holds, a misspelt one included.

prompt: Put the steps of the lesson's first pivot table in order.
hint: The source first, then the fields.
items: Click a cell of the Sales table
Keep Sales as the source and choose New Worksheet
trap: Without a cell of the table selected first, Excel has to be told the source by hand.

prompt: Suppose sale `S1003`, revenue 115, had its channel typed as `Onlnie`. What would the Channel pivot show?
hint: The pivot lists values as they are spelt.

choices.text: Online 11,143, because Excel corrects the spelling
choices.why: A pivot never corrects a value; it groups the values it finds.

choices.text: A fourth row, `Onlnie`, with 115
choices.why: Right, and Online drops to 11,028. That is why a pivot is a quick way to find misspellings.

choices.text: An error in place of the Online total
choices.why: Nothing is an error; the misspelt value is simply a group of its own.

choices.text: The same three rows, with the grand total down by 115
choices.why: The grand total still adds every row: 51,494.

prompt: Match each box of the PivotTable Fields pane to what it does.
hint: Two boxes group, one adds up, one lets records in.

pairs.right: Groups the records down the side
Groups the records across the top
Says what is added up for each group
Chooses which records count at all

prompt: In the `Grid` pivot, Product in Rows and Channel in Columns, what is the cell for `SUL1K` and `Wholesale`?
hint: A SUMIFS with two conditions gives the same.

prompt: The `Grid` pivot shows an empty cell for `CER1K` and `Shop`. What does it mean?
hint: What does a pivot put in a cell for a combination with no records?

choices.text: The pivot needs a refresh
choices.why: A refresh re-reads the data; the shop still never sold that bag.

choices.text: Nothing was sold
choices.why: Right: the shop has never sold a 1 kg bag, so there is nothing to add up.

choices.text: The value is too large to display
choices.why: A value too wide for its column shows ####, not an empty cell.

choices.text: An error in the source data for that product
choices.why: A blank in the pivot means no records, not a broken one.

prompt: With `Customer` in Filters set to `C00`, the `Wholesale` column disappears from the grid. Why?
hint: Which items does a pivot show by default?

choices.text: Filters hide the last column of a pivot
choices.why: A filter removes records; columns go only when they have none left.

choices.text: C00 never bought wholesale, so no column
choices.why: Right: a pivot shows only items with data. The column comes back with the filter set to (All).

choices.text: Wholesale customers are kept in another table
choices.why: Every sale is in Sales; the filter let only C00's in.

choices.text: The filter turned Wholesale into Online
choices.why: A filter never changes a value.

prompt: Filtered to `C00`, the Online total stays at 11,143 and the Shop total at 1,620. What does that tell you?
hint: Compare the filtered totals with the unfiltered ones.

choices.text: The filter did not apply to those two columns
choices.why: It applied to every record; those totals simply lost nothing.

choices.text: C00 buys only online
choices.why: C00 also has all 1,620 of the shop's revenue.

choices.text: Every online sale and every shop sale is a sale to C00
choices.why: Right. Only wholesale customers have codes of their own.

choices.text: The pivot needs a refresh before the filter works
choices.why: A filter works on the cache as it is; no refresh is involved.

prompt: You drag a column into Values and it arrives as **Count of** rather than **Sum of**. What does that tell you about the column?
hint: Excel picks the summary from what the column holds.

choices.text: It is the first numeric column of the table
choices.why: Position plays no part in the choice.

choices.text: It holds some text or some empty cells
choices.why: Right. Only a column holding nothing but numbers arrives as Sum.

choices.text: It holds numbers stored as dates
choices.why: Dates are numbers, and a column of them would arrive as Sum.

choices.text: It was used in another pivot first
choices.why: Each pivot chooses for itself from the data.

prompt: With `Revenue` summarised by **Count**, what does the pivot show for `Shop`?
hint: The number of shop sales.

prompt: **Sum of Price** shows 3,576 for Online. Why does the lesson call it a summary that means nothing?
hint: Try to say in words what the number is.

choices.text: Price is stored as text, so the sum is wrong
choices.why: Price is a number, and the sum is arithmetically right.

choices.text: Pivots cannot add up prices, only revenue and bags
choices.why: They can add any numeric column, which is exactly the danger.

choices.text: Adding prices of different bags answers nothing
choices.why: Right. The test is whether you can say in words what the number is.

choices.text: It should be 11,143, the Online revenue
choices.why: That is the sum of bags times price, a different column.

prompt: Shown as **% of Grand Total**, Wholesale reads 75.21%. What does that number hide?
hint: A share is a share of something.

choices.text: The size: it does not say that it is R$ 38,731
choices.why: Right. Put the amount beside the share when both matter.

choices.text: Which channel it is
choices.why: The row label still says Wholesale.

choices.text: Whether the pivot was refreshed
choices.why: An amount hides that just as much; the issue is size.

choices.text: Nothing; a share says everything an amount does
choices.why: Two channels with the same share of two different totals would read the same.

prompt: To show each channel's revenue as a share of everything sold, choose Show Values As › % of ___ Total.
hint: The total at the bottom right of the pivot.

prompt: Grouped by year, the pivot shows 35,551 for 2025 and 15,943 for 2026. Why is reading that as "revenue fell by more than half" wrong?
hint: How much of 2026 does the data cover?

choices.text: The pivot needs a refresh to include 2026
choices.why: Every sale is in the cache; the year is short, not missing.

choices.text: 2026 has only six months of data, set against twelve
choices.why: Right. Same half-year against same half-year, the fall is about a tenth.

choices.text: Excel puts some 2026 sales under 2025
choices.why: Each sale is grouped by its own date.

choices.text: The 2025 figure includes the grand total
choices.why: The grand total is a row of its own.

prompt: What is the revenue of the first half of 2025, 1 January to 30 June?
hint: The SUMIFS with two date conditions in the section.

prompt: Grouped by year and quarter, with Channel in Columns, what does the second quarter of 2026 show?
hint: Compare it with the quarter before, channel by channel.

choices.text: Every channel fell by about the same share
choices.why: Online grew; the fall is concentrated in one channel.

choices.text: Wholesale fell to 1,166; Online grew
choices.why: Right. A year total said collapse; the quarters say wholesale stopped buying.

choices.text: Revenue rose, as it does every second quarter
choices.why: Q2 2026 is the worst quarter in the data.

choices.text: The shop made up for the wholesale drop
choices.why: The shop's 111 is its smallest quarter.

prompt: `Bags` grouped from 1 to 20 by 5, with Count of Sale: how many sales fall in the `11-15` band?
hint: A COUNTIFS with two bounds checks it.

prompt: What happens if `Date` goes into Rows with no grouping at all?
hint: How many different days does the column hold?

choices.text: A row for every sale: 108 rows
choices.why: Right, since each sale is on a different day: the data again, not a summary. Grouping collects the days first.

choices.text: One row per month
choices.why: Months appear only after grouping by months.

choices.text: Excel refuses dates in Rows
choices.why: Dates are allowed; they are simply too many to read.

choices.text: A single row with the grand total
choices.why: Each distinct date is its own row.

prompt: After you change S1001's bags to 15, the check formula says 38,835 and the pivot still says 38,731. Why?
hint: What does each of them read?

choices.text: The formula is wrong until the workbook is saved
choices.why: The formula is right at once; it reads the table.

choices.text: The pivot reads its cache, a copy taken at the last refresh
choices.why: Right. Refresh, and it reads 38,835 too.

choices.text: Pivots ignore changes to existing rows and see only new ones
choices.why: A refresh picks up both.

choices.text: Excel recalculates pivots only once an hour
choices.why: Excel never refreshes a pivot on a timer by default; somebody has to.

prompt: With S1001 at 15 bags and the pivot refreshed, what is the pivot's grand total of revenue?
hint: One more bag at R$ 104.

prompt: A pivot was built on `Sales!$A$1:$H$109`. A new sale is typed in row 110 and the pivot is refreshed. What happens?
hint: What does the refresh re-read?

choices.text: The new sale appears, because a refresh reads the whole sheet
choices.why: A refresh re-reads the source, and the source stops at row 109.

choices.text: Excel widens the source by one row automatically
choices.why: Only a table grows by itself; an address never does.

choices.text: The refresh fails with an error
choices.why: It succeeds and silently leaves the sale out.

choices.text: Nothing: row 110 is outside the source
choices.why: Right. Build on the table, or widen it through Change Data Source every time.

prompt: Which of these need a Refresh before a pivot built on the `Sales` table shows them? Choose all that apply.
hint: Ask whether the change is in the data or only in the pivot's layout.

choices.text: Editing the bags of an existing sale
choices.why: The cache still holds the old value.

choices.text: Adding a sale at the bottom of the table
choices.why: The table grows at once; the cache only at the next refresh.

choices.text: Moving Channel from Rows to Columns
choices.why: A layout change is computed from the cache the pivot already has.

choices.text: Correcting the spelling of a channel
choices.why: It is a change in the data, so the misspelt group stays until a refresh.

choices.text: Changing Sum of Revenue to Count
choices.why: Another summary of the same cache; nothing new has to be read.

prompt: Which of these questions can **not** be answered by moving fields between the four boxes of a pivot built on `Sales`?
hint: Three of them are a grouping and a sum or a count; one needs a ratio of two sums.

choices.text: Revenue by customer and product
choices.why: Customer in Rows, Product in Columns, Revenue in Values.

choices.text: The number of sales per channel in each year
choices.why: Date grouped by years in Rows, Channel in Columns, Count.

choices.text: The average price paid per bag, for each product
choices.why: Right. That is total revenue divided by total bags, a ratio of two sums; lesson 11 does it with a calculated field.

choices.text: Each product's share of its channel's revenue
choices.why: Show Values As › % of Column Total.

prompt: A pivot of revenue by year and a `SUMIFS` for 2026 on the same `Sales` table disagree. What should you do first?
hint: The lesson names the commonest cause by far.

choices.text: Rebuild the pivot from scratch on a new sheet
choices.why: That costs minutes and finds nothing a refresh would not; Refresh is the step that re-reads the data.

choices.text: Trust the pivot, because Excel wrote it
choices.why: The pivot is the one reading a copy; the formula reads the table now.

choices.text: Refresh the pivot, then compare again
choices.why: Right. If they still disagree after a refresh, then look for a filter or a wrong condition.

choices.text: Delete the formula, since two numbers confuse readers
choices.why: The disagreement is the information; the formula is the check.

prompt: With Customer filtered to `C00`, what is the grand total of revenue in the `Grid` pivot?
hint: `=SUMIFS(Sales[Revenue], Sales[Customer], "C00")`
